title: NETCONF and RESTCONF: structured, transactional configuration

videos.script: A change has five lines. The router accepts the first two and refuses the third. Now it runs a configuration nobody designed. {{half}} NETCONF was written so that never happens. {{netconf}} You edit a working copy, called the candidate. The device checks it against a model. Then one commit makes all of it real, or none of it. {{candidate}} In this lesson you open a session by hand and read the XML the protocol speaks. Then you use ncclient to read, edit, validate and commit. {{session}} You send a change with a mistake in it and watch the whole transaction refused. You disable an uplink with a confirmed commit, confirm nothing, and watch the device put it back after ten seconds. {{confirmed}} Two sessions compete for a lock. And the same data comes out of RESTCONF, as JSON, over HTTPS. {{restconf}} The device is nc1. Its configuration is managed by Clixon, and it is shaped by two standard models. {{nc1}}
